court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division
holding_summary: A married woman authorized by her husband to take boarders and receive pay may recover for board furnished as her own separate business, notwithstanding that the boarder may have paid her husband without her authority. The court held the evidence was sufficient to submit that theory to the jury, though it affirmed the trial court's discretionary order setting aside the verdict and granting a new trial.

quotes.text: She attended to the household duties, carrying on no separate business save that upon a few occasions she had taken a boarder into the family and received the pay therefor.

If this was the true state of affairs she is entitled to recover, notwithstanding the fact that the defendant may have paid her husband therefor, if such payment was made without authority from her and after she had • repeatedly asserted her claim against him.
While we have reached the conclusion that it was proper to set aside the verdict and grant a new trial herein, we think the evidence was sufficient to require the case to be submitted to the jury.

notes: Occupancy at issue spanned a longer period (defendant lived in the family for about two years after majority, then returned for a final seven-week stretch found supportable as an express contract); coded duration as 'weeks' for that final contract-supported segment.

court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division
holding_summary: A son-in-law who received his mother-in-law into the home he shared with his wife could not recover from her estate for board and lodging furnished, absent proof of an express contract to pay. The court held that the law does not imply an obligation to pay for board and lodging furnished by a relative who takes in a family member, and any parol contract must be shown by disinterested or corroborating testimony. The claimant's proof, resting mainly on his own and his wife's testimony, was held insufficient.

quotes.text: The theory of the claimant, however, is that the intestate agreed to pay a weekly sum for her board and lodging.
The law should not imply an obligation to pay, inasmuch as the claimant is a son-in-law of the intestate and received her into the home occupied by him and his wife.

In order to entitle a son-in-law to recover from the estate of his mother-in-law moneys alleged to be due for board and lodging furnished to the decedent, a contract to pay therefor must be established, either by written evidence, or, if established by parol, it must be by the testimony of disinterested witnesses, or the contract must be corroborated by them in all substantial particulars.

notes: Family-lodging context (son-in-law/mother-in-law) rather than the stranger-lodger scenario at the core of the project's inquiry; coded mixed/lodging because the court treats board-for-pay as legally cognizable but declines to imply it within a household-family relationship absent proof; duration left unclear because the opinion describes an extended, unspecified multi-year stay rather than a discrete nights/weeks/months period.
